text: Nicotine, the principal addictive alkaloid in tobacco, is rapidly absorbed through the lungs and mucosal tissues and reaches the brain within seconds after smoking [ 10 ]. Following absorption, nicotine is extensively metabolized in the liver, with approximately 70–80% converted into cotinine, its primary and more stable metabolite. Cotinine is a well-established biomarker known for its stability and specificity to tobacco exposure, making it a valuable tool for accurate measurement [ 10 ].
source_label: Biomarker-based assessment of tobacco smoke exposure in Saudi females via analysis of urinary cotinine level
